routes.label: Apply Ptolemy to four selected vertices
Use a 60° rotation and collinear lengths
Split the longest diagonal using an equilateral triangle

question:
If \(a,\) \(b\) and \(d\) are the lengths of a side, a shortest diagonal and a longest diagonal, respectively, of a regular nonagon (see adjoining figure), then

[Figure 1](figures/1977_AMC_12_Q30_question_fig1.svg)
solution:
The nine equally spaced vertices suggest using every third vertex to form an equilateral triangle. Label the vertices consecutively \(V_0,V_1,\ldots,V_8\) around the circumcircle, and set
\[
A=V_0,\quad P=V_1,\quad B=V_3,\quad C=V_6.
\]
Each interval between consecutive vertices subtends \(360^\circ/9=40^\circ\) at the center. The chords \(AB,BC,CA\) each span three intervals, so \(ABC\) is equilateral. Also, \(AP=a\), \(PB=b\), and \(PC=d\): these chords span one, two, and four intervals along their minor arcs, respectively.

We will split \(PC\) into lengths \(a\) and \(b\). The arc \(AC\) that avoids \(P\) spans three intervals, or \(120^\circ\). By the inscribed angle theorem,
\[
\angle APC=60^\circ.
\]
Choose \(X\) on \(PC\) with \(PX=PA=a\). This point lies strictly between \(P\) and \(C\), since a longest diagonal is longer than a side. Now \(\angle APX=60^\circ\) and \(PA=PX\), so \(APX\) is equilateral. In particular, \(AX=AP=a\) and \(\angle PAX=60^\circ\).

The arc \(PC\) avoiding \(A\) spans five intervals, while the arc \(PB\) avoiding \(A\) spans two. Thus
\[
\angle CAP=100^\circ,
\qquad \angle BAP=40^\circ.
\]
Because \(X\) is inside side \(PC\) of triangle \(APC\), ray \(AX\) lies inside \(\angle CAP\). Therefore
\[
\angle CAX=100^\circ-60^\circ=40^\circ.
\]
Triangles \(ABP\) and \(ACX\) have \(AB=AC\), \(AP=AX\), and equal included angles \(\angle BAP=\angle CAX\). They are congruent by SAS, giving \(CX=BP=b\). Consequently,
\[
d=PC=PX+XC=\boxed{a+b},
\]
which is choice \(\boxed{\text{A}}\).
